Looking at this problem, I need to find the maximum of P(8) where P is a polynomial of degree ≤ 6 and P(1),...,P(7) is a permutation of {1,...,7}.

## Key Tool: Finite Differences

For any polynomial of degree ≤ 6, the **7th forward difference vanishes**:

$$\Delta^7 P(1) = \sum_{k=0}^{7} (-1)^{7-k}\binom{7}{k} P(1+k) = 0$$

Expanding:

$$-P(1)+7P(2)-21P(3)+35P(4)-35P(5)+21P(6)-7P(7)+P(8)=0$$

Solving for P(8):

$$P(8) = 1\cdot P(1) - 7\cdot P(2) + 21\cdot P(3) - 35\cdot P(4) + 35\cdot P(5) - 21\cdot P(6) + 7\cdot P(7)$$

## Existence Check

Any assignment of 7 values to P(1),...,P(7) determines a **unique** polynomial of degree ≤ 6 (Lagrange interpolation through 7 points). So every permutation of {1,...,7} is realizable, and P(8) is uniquely determined by the formula above. The only freedom is which value goes to which input.

## Optimization via Rearrangement Inequality

The coefficients for positions 1–7 are:

| Position | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|----------|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Coefficient | 1 | -7 | 21 | -35 | 35 | -21 | 7 |

Sorted ascending: **-35, -21, -7, 1, 7, 21, 35** (positions 4, 6, 2, 1, 7, 3, 5).

By the **Rearrangement Inequality**, the sum $\sum c_i \cdot P(i)$ is maximized when the values are sorted in the **same order** as the coefficients (both ascending). So assign the smallest value to the most negative coefficient, and the largest to the most positive:

| Coefficient | -35 | -21 | -7 | 1 | 7 | 21 | 35 |
|-------------|-----|-----|-----|---|---|----|----|
| Position | 4 | 6 | 2 | 1 | 7 | 3 | 5 |
| P value | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |

This gives: **P(1)=4, P(2)=3, P(3)=6, P(4)=1, P(5)=7, P(6)=2, P(7)=5**.

## Computation

$$P(8) = 1(4) - 7(3) + 21(6) - 35(1) + 35(7) - 21(2) + 7(5)$$

$$= 4 - 21 + 126 - 35 + 245 - 42 + 35$$

$$= 312$$

## Verification of the Permutation

The assigned values {4, 3, 6, 1, 7, 2, 5} = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} ✓ — a valid permutation.

## Conclusion

The maximum possible value of P(8) is:

$$\boxed{312}$$
